extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: MMMU is a benchmark consisting of 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, and focus on advanced perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. They were advised to select questions without immediately available answers. The process involved three stages: (1) selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on whether visual inputs are commonly adopted, (2) recruiting university students specializing in these majors to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources or create new questions based on their expertise, (3) quality control through lexical overlap and URL similarity checks for duplicates, format and typo checking by co-authors, and categorizing problems into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), with very easy problems excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Quality control was performed through three stages: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity to identify duplicates, which were then manually reviewed by authors, (2) format and typo checking by co-authors to ensure standardized format, (3) difficulty categorization into four levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard) with approximately 10% of very easy problems excluded. Human expert evaluation was conducted with 90 college senior students (3 per subject) completing 30 questions each in their corresponding subjects (900 validation questions total), achieving accuracies ranging from 76.2% (worst) to 88.6% (best).
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 annotation per item for question collection; 3 expert annotations per subject for validation (90 students total evaluating 900 validation questions, with 3 students per subject evaluating 30 questions each)
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects; 90 college senior students for expert evaluation representing 30 different subjects
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The benchmark focuses on college-level subjects which might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The selection of subjects was based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted, which ruled out subjects like law and linguistics.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The benchmark combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions to balance complexity and practicality. Approximately 10% of problems classified as 'very easy' were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU marks a critical milestone towards Expert AGI (Level 3), which denotes AI systems reaching 'at least 90th percentile of skilled adults' in a broad range of tasks. This has significant implications for job displacement and economic disruption. The benchmark is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI and is of both intellectual and societal importance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: MMMU is designed for zero-shot evaluation to assess the capability of models to generate accurate answers without fine-tuning. The benchmark is intended to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It aims to push the boundaries of what LMMs can achieve and prove instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: MMMU is divided into a few-shot development set (5 questions per subject), a validation set (approximately 900 questions), and a test set (10.5K questions). A live-updating leaderboard is available at https://mmmu-benchmark.github.io/#leaderboard.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data quality control through three stages: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity to identify duplicates with manual review, (2) format and typo checking by co-authors with standardized format enforcement, (3) difficulty categorization into four levels with exclusion of approximately 10% very easy problems not meeting design criteria

name.evidence: We introduce MMMU: a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.

description.evidence: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To further control the quality of our data, we perform two steps of data cleaning. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking. This step requires authors to ensure adherence to a standardized format, undertaking necessary corrections where deviations are found. In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.
